newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ arch-rivals sign deal to bury the hatchet.
newsitem.headline: NZ arch-rivals sign deal to bury the hatchet.

text.p: Two former arch-rivals of New Zealand politics set aside old scores and signed a coalition pact on Wednesday, but the New Zealand dollar slipped on concern about the powerful role of populist Winston Peters.
Peters and Prime Minister Jim Bolger promised stable government, more cash for hospitals and schools, and a better deal for Maori in a new government of the centre-right.

Peters, shunning an alternative pact with the Labour Party, announced on Tuesday his New Zealand First Party would join the conservative National Party in government after two months of intensive negotiations.
He buried the hatchet with Bolger, the man who fired him from his cabinet in 1991, saying personalities must be set aside in the new coalition era.

"We believe the coalition agreement builds on the economic change of the past six years by addressing new economic, governmental and social priorities indicated by voters at the general election," the two leaders said in a statement.
The new government will boost spending by NZ$5 billion (US$3.5 billion) in the next three years, with the lion's share to go in the sensitive areas of health and education.
Peters, who has frequently called for a fall in interest rates and a lower New Zealand dollar to help exporters, will hold the powerful roles of treasurer and deputy prime minister.
Labour, crushed by the failure to reach a deal with Peters, said it had refused to give him the key economic portfolio. Leader Helen Clark said Bolger was in Peters' thrall.
"It's not just that Mr Bolger has a tiger by the tail, but he is being led around like a poodle now," she said.
The New Zealand dollar has fallen about a cent to just above 69.5 U.S. cents in the 24 hours since the deal was announced.

"The markets are struggling with the credibility of Peters as treasurer given his views on foreign investment and the relative value of the exchange rate and the level of expenditure he desires," said National Bank chief foreign exchange dealer Stu Nattrass.

Peters said exporters would be pleased by the currency's reaction and a fall in interest rates, and there was no need for the market to panic. The stockmarket rose, and rating agency Moody's said it saw no change to New Zealand's credit standing.
Details of the coalition deal made clear the concessions secured by Peters.

A NZ$1 billion cap on settlements of Maori land claims was removed, and new Maori health and education initatives were announced -- key points for the influential group of Maori MPs in New Zealand First.

The new coalition said it was desirable for New Zealanders to control important national assets. Electricity generators, New Zealand Post, the TV1 channel and Radio New Zealand would not be put up for sale.

Immigration would be held at current levels, with a "clampdown on refugee scams". Children under five would get free medical treatment, while elderly people would see the removal of a highly unpopular tax surcharge on pensioners' income.

In a separate develoment, police said they were investigating an overnight incident in which Bolger's official limousine was torched and extensively damaged. The diplomatic protection squad said it was stepping up his security.
